hook.text: A company creates dozens of smaller budgets. They all roll up into one master plan.

buildup.text: The master budget combines sales, production, purchasing, labor, overhead, and capital budgets.

discovery.text: It produces a projected income statement, balance sheet, and cash flow statement for the period.

twist.text: If the sales budget is wrong, every other budget built on it will be wrong too.

climax.text: The master budget is the company's financial blueprint—every department contributes a piece.

punchline.text: One plan unites every department's numbers.

quiz.question: What does a master budget combine?
options: All individual department budgets into one plan

details.summary: The master budget is the comprehensive financial plan that ties together all of a company's individual budgets—sales, production, purchasing, labor, overhead, and capital—into one cohesive projection of financial performance.
details.whyItMatters: Without a master budget, departments plan in isolation and their numbers don't add up. The master budget forces coordination, reveals resource conflicts, and gives leadership a complete financial picture.
takeaways: The master budget starts with the sales budget—everything else flows from expected sales
It includes both operating budgets (revenue and expenses) and financial budgets (cash, capital, pro-forma statements)
The cash budget is often the most critical component because it reveals whether the company can fund its plans

faq.question: What is a master budget?
faq.answer: A master budget is the complete set of interconnected budgets that projects a company's financial performance for a period. It starts with the sales forecast and flows through production, materials, labor, overhead, selling expenses, and culminates in pro-forma financial statements.

faq.question: Why does the master budget start with the sales budget?
faq.answer: Everything depends on how much the company expects to sell. Production quantities are driven by sales demand, material purchases by production needs, labor by production schedules, and overhead by activity levels. Sales is the independent variable that drives all others.
